title: Control Statements: Using If-Else Conditionals & Logic
summary: Introduces control flow with if/else: a condition in parentheses decides which block runs. Applied to the love calculator so a high score gets a special message.

concepts.heading: Control flow and conditionals
points: Control flow means the program takes different paths depending on current conditions.
if evaluates a condition. When it is true the block that follows runs; else holds the block for when it is false.
Syntax: if (condition) { ... } else { ... }. The condition sits in parentheses, each branch in curly braces.
Convention is to put the opening brace on the same line as if and else, which keeps long blocks readable.
Only one of the two blocks runs for any given evaluation.

concepts.heading: Conditions in the love calculator
points: Equality is tested with three equals signs: loveScore === 100. This only triggers for one value in a hundred, so it is awkward to test.
Testing a range is more practical, using a comparator such as greater than: loveScore > 70.
(Extra) A single = assigns a value and must not be used as a comparison inside if.

task.name: Add a special message to the love calculator
task.starting_point: The love calculator from the previous lecture.
task.goal: Show a different alert when the score is high.
steps: Keep the prompts and the 1-100 loveScore calculation.
Wrap the alert in if (loveScore > 70) with an extended message.
Put the plain message in the else block.
Run several times to see both branches.
task.expected_result: Scores above 70 show the special message; others show the plain one.

pitfalls: Using = instead of === in a condition.
Testing for a single exact value when a range is wanted.
Forgetting braces or parentheses around the condition.

playground.coverage: Covers the love-score branch, else if chains, ordering, truthy/falsy and the ternary.

Demo idea: a button repeatedly generating scores and tallying which branch ran.
